The team then noticed that co-op horror games with comic elements were popular on Steam. That genre has a culture of laughing together at players' failures. From this came the idea of mimicry: rather than combat, imitating a teammate's movement and voice to make other players doubt whether a companion is real or a monster could become a new kind of fun. The demo came together in three months and ranked 4th among the world's most-played demos at Steam Next Fest in January 2025.

Large language models also came up. Lee Gi-mun explained that the behavior part and the voice part are separate. Behavior analysis feeds over 4,000 pieces of information into a neural network, which doesn't suit an LLM, and since MIMESIS deals only with its own specific information, there's no need for an expensive LLM. The voice part uses recorded voices rather than synthesis.

Going forward, the major update MIMESIS 3.0 aims to expand the idea so that players doubt the entire game. Lee Gi-mun said the studio plans to release one more title within 2026 and is also considering using new technologies such as “overhearing AI.”

A behind-the-scenes video documenting the making of Supergirl was hastily taken down. It had failed to win people over. Far from showcasing the crew's craft, everyone's attention locked onto a single moment in the video: a part where the team appeared to have used AI to create concept art for one character.

blocks.cap: Lobo in Supergirl

blocks.x: In the scene in question, a few crew members look over several versions of Lobo, played by Jason Momoa. Rather than poring over carefully hand-drawn concept art, it looks like AI-generated images that overlay various design ideas onto Momoa's face. Almost no one is happy about the possibility that this was part of the creative process.
The video focused on how the character Lobo was realized for the new Supergirl film. The official upload, however, can no longer be viewed. It has been switched to private.

This came after a clip from the video spread widely online. In that clip, the crew looks over concept art that appears clearly AI-generated in order to settle on one element of Lobo's design. Many people voiced disappointment and anger that generative AI had been anywhere near Supergirl's production.

No evidence of AI use elsewhere has surfaced, but the incident has cast suspicion on other parts of the film too. Even if it was limited to concept art, there's still a chance other characters got the same treatment. The earliest work may have been done by hand, with AI used only for finishing touches on the design, but that's disappointing all the same. Filmmaking has run perfectly well on human creativity alone. It's also hard to argue that a comic-book movie needs AI reference art.

It hasn't been confirmed that the AI backlash is why the video was taken down. Still, it's the most plausible reason. That was, after all, the part of the video that drew the most attention. So what happens now? Will they re-upload it with that part cut? It's too late for that. A statement explaining how generative AI was used seems more likely, and once the fuss dies down, the video will probably quietly go public again.
As of 10:25 p.m. UK time, a correction was added to the article, noting that the use of generative AI is suspected, not confirmed.
One thing remains clear: big studios still have a long way to go before AI slop becomes normal.

Yesterday, the Twitch streaming community learned that its content was being used to train Amazon's AI models. The way they found out wasn't exactly above board. Rather than issuing a formal notice and asking creators for permission, Twitch had turned the feature on by default on streamer accounts and quietly buried the opt-out deep inside the platform's security settings.

blocks.cap: Image: Twitch / Shutterstock

blocks.x: In a livestream explaining the AI training program and answering the community's questions and concerns, Twitch's Chief Product Officer Mike Minton gave a striking answer when asked why the setting was opt-out rather than opt-in: “If it were opt-in, nobody would turn it on. Well, honestly, that's the answer. That's why it's on by default.”

Gamers dislike generative AI. People who make games dislike it too. And Twitch is now watching, in real time, that streamers who play and broadcast games dislike it as well. Social media is flooded with posts from streamers angry that their content is being used for AI training — and that the setting is on by default. Critics have called it deceptive, since no one can turn off a setting they don't even know exists.
Streamers are fighting back in whatever ways they can. The biggest one is simply telling each other what's going on and where to turn the setting off.

The annoying part is that opting out only works on your own channel. Even if you turn it off on your channel, stepping into another streamer's chat who hasn't opted out means whatever is said there still gets used for AI training. So streamers started using the tag “aioptedout” to signal that a channel is safe to chat in.

Twitch's feedback forum has also become an outlet. The top-voted suggestion in the “Creators and Stream Features” category is “Make all AI features opt-in, with opt-out as the default.” It had gathered 15,714 votes as of this writing. AI may be everywhere these days, but at least in the gaming community, players are loudly saying this isn't it.
Nearly half of respondents named AI-assisted development as the biggest industry trend of the next three years.

blocks.cap: Image: Gamescom

blocks.x: Gamescom Dev released the results of its annual speaker survey. 83% of respondents said AI affects team structure or productivity.

Among the 100 speakers surveyed, nearly half named AI-assisted development as the most important industry trend of the next three years. It was followed by hardware and RAM prices at 28%, the creator economy at 7%, and user-generated content at 5%.
30% said they want to use AI minimally in development, down from 33% last year. In contrast, 34% said code and production benefit most from AI assistance.

On jobs, 36% said roles would change rather than team sizes shrinking, while 33% expected teams to get smaller. 14% said individual output would increase, and 17% said there would be no workforce cuts.
More than half of respondents named economic uncertainty as the industry's biggest challenge. Market saturation (38%), discoverability (35%), and rising development costs (30%) followed.
To improve discoverability, respondents pointed to greater transparency in platform algorithms (32%), better store recommendations (22%), and more curated editorial coverage (21%).
For future opportunities, 37% cited smaller development teams, followed by community building and new publishing models, each at 15%.

Opinions were split on which business or revenue model will dominate the market over the next three years. Digital and packaged premium games led at 29%, followed by live services at 24% and item-based free-to-play at 21%.

It's been alleged that publisher Saber Interactive made heavy use of generative AI on its upcoming driving sim Rideshare “Stimulator,” even replacing some staff with bots like ChatGPT, without disclosing AI use on its Steam store page.

blocks.cap: Image: Saber Interactive

blocks.x: Rideshare “Stimulator” first became known through a trailer Saber and developer Unigine released on July 30. On August 11, former lead writer Stella Sacco reacted to the news on Bluesky, saying Saber had buried its AI use.

“I didn't even know it had been announced. I was the lead writer on this game. And Saber replaced me with ChatGPT partway through development,” Sacco said. “The passenger voices were all AI too. Either they changed direction partway through, or they're just not disclosing it on Steam.”
Sacco also pointed to a post she made on December 21, 2023: “I got replaced at work on a game I was working on. By ChatGPT.”
Her LinkedIn history states she was at Saber from July 2023 to July 2024, as “lead writer on several titles in Saber's portfolio, including STUNTMAN HOLLYWOOD.”
Rideshare “Stimulator” bills itself as a driving simulator layered with a rideshare business sim. Players plot routes across a city, talk to passengers, and chase a high driver rating.

“Dodge traffic, follow the rules, race against the clock, and drop off quirky passengers, each with their own story that's interesting, funny, or just plain weird,” reads the Steam description. A newly created Saber website page uses the same wording.

Conspicuously missing from that Steam page is an AI disclosure. Valve requires games that use generative AI in “content that is shipped with the game and is consumed by players” to disclose that on Steam. According to the Steamworks content survey documentation, that includes “artwork, sound, narrative, localization, and more.”

Many developers have told GamesRadar+ that they support Valve's generative AI policy. There is opposition within the industry, though, with Epic Games and Epic Games Store boss Tim Sweeney a notable example.
The allegation has already spread to the YouTube comments on the public trailer, and to the PS5 version's video as well.
“'Replaced the writers and voice actors with AI!' Got it.” reads one comment posted an hour before this article's deadline.
“AI writing with AI voice.” read another comment posted an hour before that.
“No AI disclosure on the Steam page, planning to fix that? Seems like at least one writer got pushed out by chatgpt.” reads yet another recent comment.
GamesRadar+ has asked Saber Interactive for comment on Rideshare “Stimulator's” AI use and policy.
In a separate, unrelated note, Saber CEO Matt Karch recently confirmed that Rideshare “Simulator” does in fact contain a joke aimed at Gearbox CEO Randy Pitchford.
As games increasingly adopt real-time inference, memory usage and runtime efficiency now matter as much as the quality of the model itself.

Recorded at Unreal Fest Chicago 2026, this talk covers how Databiomes has optimized AI models for use in actual game runtimes, working closely with AMD to balance fidelity, performance, energy efficiency, and platform constraints.

Databiomes and AMD share lessons learned from moving offline-trained models into real-time execution in Unreal Engine. That includes strategies for easing memory pressure, ways to cut latency, and how to scale across a wide range of hardware spanning CPUs, GPUs, and NPUs.

The talk also shows how AMD's technology and plugins help trim runtime costs further, the goal being AI features that fit within real-world performance and memory budgets. After watching, it becomes clearer what it actually takes to ship AI in games today.
Posted by the Unreal Engine channel on August 7, 2026, the video runs a little over 33 minutes.
Game Science is taking its time making Black Myth: Zhong Kui.

On Weibo, Yang Qi, art director of the Black Myth series and co-founder of Game Science, answered a fan's question about whether AI would be used to speed up development. “We'll stay away from AI-generated content at the design and asset stages.” According to a translation shared by a Reset Era user, he said: “Not out of resistance — we're simply trying to hold our ground until the end.”

blocks.cap: Image: Game Science

blocks.x: To expand on his thinking, he brought up Nolan's latest epic, The Odyssey. “At a time when digital filmmaking and 3D post-production seem to have hit a dead end, look at Nolan,” Qi wrote.

“He's doing great. He's even shaking things up using older techniques,” he continued. “There's no ‘last train’ we absolutely have to catch. It's fine to stay at a small inn for a while. Besides, there's plenty of time for things like AI. No need to rush.”

That's welcome news, since technologies like generative AI and chatbots are becoming more and more common across the industry. Tomb Raider: Legacy of Atlantis, Call of Duty: Black Ops 7, and Kingdom Hearts are three cases confirmed or suspected to have used generative AI assets in some form, and all three drew considerable backlash.

Stellar Blade: Blood Rain also used an AI music video as part of its promotion, and its creative director sees the technology as essential to the Korean game development scene. It's reassuring to see Game Science hold out against that trend and lean solely on human-led creation.
Still, the possibility that it could enter the pipeline later lingers. One can only hope the negative reaction surrounding Stellar Blade gives Game Science enough reason to hold back.
Amazon has released the first long-form drama made entirely with AI on any major global streaming platform.

blocks.cap: Image credit: GamesBeat

blocks.x: The period drama “Castle Walls” landed on Amazon Prime Video on August 12. Two 15-minute episodes were released together on the same day, making it the world's first all-AI television series. Production was handled by AI Yapım, the AI division of Ay Yapım, a three-time International Emmy-winning Turkish production company. The story is drawn from the legend of Alamut Castle, the central setting of Assassin's Creed Mirage.

The visuals were produced by AYDNA, an in-house video diffusion model trained only on Ay Yapım's own content catalog, to which it holds the rights. AI Yapım said in its press release that this was a deliberate choice to avoid data scraped from outside sources, at a time when the industry is under scrutiny over the provenance of training data. The pipeline combined prompt enhancement, creative development and a proprietary storyboarding system, with AYDNA generating the finished footage. Dubbing for each language, however, was done by human voice actors, and the performances were not AI-generated.

blocks.cap: One of the hand-drawn images made while creating “Castle Walls.”

blocks.x: There's roughly a two-year gap between the two episodes by AI development standards, and it shows on screen. The first episode was built shot by shot using an inpainting technique that predates today's mainstream image-generation models — a labor-intensive older method of piecing together frames one by one. The second episode added more advanced generative AI tools to the pipeline. Rather than appearing as separate works released years apart, that shift plays out side by side within a single series.

Even though AI generated the visuals, all narrative and editorial decisions were made by people. The creative team was led by writers Kerem Deren and Çisil Hazal Tenim, who also worked together on the internationally distributed drama “El Turco.” Before AI entered the process, human artists hand-drew sketches of characters and locations to establish the backgrounds and character designs first. Those sketches were included in the press kit, which AI Yapım said was meant to show where human input sits within the production process.

The production pedigree is solid for an AI series. Parent company Ay Yapım is a three-time International Emmy winner, with credits including “Endless Love (Kara Sevda),” the first Turkish drama to win an International Emmy; “Şahsiyet,” which earned Haluk Bilginer a Best Actor award; and “Family Secrets (Yargı).” AI Yapım also runs WAIFF Turkey, the Turkish chapter of the World AI Film Festival, and is listed as an AI production capability partner for the International Emmy's education program.

For gamers, the Assassin's Creed connection serves as the entry point. Alamut Castle was already fictionalized in Ubisoft's Mirage, and here it becomes the thread that ties the drama's story together. “Castle Walls” is now streaming worldwide on Amazon Prime Video.

There's a game that stayed hidden from Western audiences for a long time: the Super Famicom title Kamaitachi no Yoru. Remakes have been localized before, but the original had never been properly translated — until translator and programmer But Thou Must did it without using any AI at all.

blocks.cap: Some ports replaced the silhouettes with anime characters.

blocks.x: The title translates roughly to “Night of the Sickle Weasel.” A kamaitachi is a yokai with blade-like arms that rides on whirlwinds. The game runs almost entirely on text, and because Chunsoft labeled the genre a “sound novel,” it reads more like a book than most visual novels. Protagonist Tooru and his girlfriend Mari get trapped at the Spur mountain lodge during a ski trip, and murders follow one after another in the snowstorm. There are about 40 bad endings, and players have to get through all of them to reach the real culprit. It sold 750,000 copies in 1994 and later became a foundational work for the visual novel genre.

Translating it was also a technical battle. The original Japanese version capped name entry at six characters. “Six characters was enough for the default names, Tooru and Mari. But where you have to enter the name of who you think the killer is, six characters wasn't enough,” But Thou Must said on Discord. They wrote their own assembly code to extend the culprit's name to ten characters, and Tooru and Mari's to seven.

They drew a clear line against AI translation. “I don't agree with the attitude that an AI fan translation is 'better than nothing.' If it's a game's first translation, that patch becomes the player's first and probably only experience of it. Even if a human-made fan translation comes along later, most people won't care — they've already played the game.”

blocks.cap: Innocent Tears, an original Xbox game that was Japan-only.

blocks.x: Patches for Innocent Tears and London Spirit Detectives came out the same week. Innocent Tears' GitHub page reads, “No AI was used in this patch. Only pure stupidity.” The English patch for Kowloon's Gate, released earlier this year, belongs to the same lineage.

blocks.cap: London Spirit Detectives, a PlayStation RPG released by Bandai in 1999.

blocks.x: bigbanana23, the hacker behind London Spirit Detectives, isn't opposed to AI itself but is skeptical about using it for this kind of work. “Once you start leaning on AI for this, you lose the chance to develop your own skills, and the pool of people who actually understand the process behind this hobby slowly thins out.” For translator Aishsha, it was more personal — they lost a mass of clients who switched to AI chasing speed and lower cost, and several of them came back saying, “please look at this mess.”

Even so, this is a golden age for fan translation. Kowloon's Gate translator _dk says feng shui and Taoist theory aren't properly laid out on the English-language internet, so there's little for an LLM to scrape, and that context simply couldn't be left to AI. “As long as the community doesn't settle for 'good enough,' projects will keep coming,” said Innocent Tears translator SnowyAria.

Over the past few weeks, a Pokemon PC port called Gen1Recomp spread quickly. Mods that turn the original Game Boy RPG into a 3D voxel world played a big part in that. It launched supporting Pokemon Red, Blue and Yellow, and has now added beta support for Pokemon Gold. Developer BryanThaBoi also answered in detail how the project used AI — and that answer might not be what people expected.

blocks.cap: Image credit: Nintendo / @Charmi

blocks.x: Gen1Recomp works much like other classic-game PC ports we've seen before. It runs the classic Pokemon games exactly as remembered, the way an emulator would, but with added graphics options. If you want to zoom the camera way out to see the map from far away, you can do that.

What's really exciting is the room for modding. Gen1Recomp already has a ton of mods attached to it, including some that turn the entire game world into a 3D voxel map, opening up a completely new perspective. That novelty is what pushed Gen1Recomp into the spotlight almost overnight.

If you dislike seeing AI tangled up in fan projects, there's bad news. Gen1Recomp was made with AI — or more precisely, made with the help of AI, and BryanThaBoi is very insistent on that distinction.

“You see this? Pretty cool, right? And this is just the start. Modders have already put out over 100 new mods. On top of that, there are 6 translations in the most widely used languages, with more on the way.” The developer posted this on August 3.

“No, this recomp wasn't 'made with Claude.'” That's a statement the developer posted on Discord. “Did I use AI? Yes. Those are two different statements, but the problem is that most people hear them as one. Specifically, that using AI means vibe coding. That's not true. It can be, but not in this case.”

What BryanThaBoi means by vibe coding is inexperienced developers using AI to paper over gaps in their own knowledge. That's the same kind of thing the developers of the PS3 emulator RPCS3 were trying to block earlier this year when they decided to stop accepting AI-generated code submissions altogether.

BryanThaBoi insists their own use of AI is different — an experienced software developer using AI as a supporting tool, the way they would in their day job. It's the same spirit as Valve head Gabe Newell calling AI developers' “cheat code.”

“When someone asks me point blank, 'is this AI,' I've answered no — because it's not what they mean by it,” BryanThaBoi said. “The moment you say 'I used AI,' people assume vibe coding, that you're hands-off and don't even know how to develop. That's not what happened here. So it's nearly impossible to answer people who've already closed their minds on this topic, or who don't understand it at all and are just angry that AI touched anything.”

To people who get angry at their stance, BryanThaBoi responds with a single GIF. It reads “eat a shoe,” and you can probably guess what it shows. Making the position clear counts for something, but this response probably won't sit well with those who reject AI outright.

New technology always runs into the same problem. Cutting-edge tech moves fast, on a timescale of a few years, while humans — soft, fleshy bodies carrying complex bureaucracies and legal systems — move at a glacial pace. That exact scene is playing out with generative AI.

blocks.cap: Image credit: Larian

blocks.x: For a few years now, the games industry has been pouring out excited talk: that AI would let small studios make big games, that soon it would generate concept art, music and game dialogue on its own. Naturally, the tired phrase “democratizing art” never failed to come up.

In practice, generative AI is closer to a plagiarism machine. It often spits out near-copies, and even when it doesn't, running it requires countless pieces of copyrighted work (some of which, at times, literally need to be burned away). That legal heat has scared game companies, lawyer Haley MacLean said in an interview with GamesRadar+.

MacLean, who handles corporate IP at Voyer Law with a focus on games, says AI-ban clauses have especially surged in the past year. “It's flipped completely, especially over the last year. Two or three years ago you'd see it only occasionally … now even small, bare-bones publishing studios are like, 'let's just put it in to cover ourselves.'”

“So now it's just boilerplate. In fact, if I come across a contract without a generative AI clause, and the publisher is also making assets, I'll push to add one — because we need it locked in that the publisher can't use generative AI for the game's marketing, porting, or QA.”

Even looked at through the cold eyes of capital, this isn't surprising. There's tension between platforms and developers over clearing AI slop off their own shores. Platforms recommend attaching big, clear disclosures so users can filter out the junk, but the developers who actually attach those disclosures end up sinking because of it.

In June, a data analyst found that AI disclosures cut the number of reviews a game receives by as much as 53% and make overall ratings more negative. MacLean says that's why the attitude “I don't want to use generative AI because the community will hate it” has become so widespread.

To introduce its beta AI features, Unity brought in Stacey Haffner — a former Microsoft principal developer advocate who has spent more than a decade making indie games and posting development tutorials on YouTube every other week. She shared five tips for bringing GitHub Copilot into Unity work.

First, don't fight the context window — structure the work around its limits. “The context window is the AI's working memory for a session, and it has a limit.” Depending on the underlying model, performance can start to sag even before that limit is reached, and if you compress a session after it's already sagged, that sagging state becomes the new baseline. For big features, a main thread breaks the work into small pieces and directs it, spinning up separate implementation and verification agents and running them until they pass.

blocks.cap: The Copilot chat panel drafting an implementation plan for a modular quest system.

blocks.x: Second, set up the project environment ahead of time. Putting configuration files in the project's .github folder lets you tune a general model's behavior to this domain. Always-on Custom Instructions hold defaults like coding rules, the Unity engine version, and the rendering pipeline. Agents are split into domain-expert personas, like shaders or UI Toolkit, while Skills are modular instructions that only get called in when the relevant task comes up, saving memory.

blocks.cap: The customization screen for managing agents, skills, and instructions.

blocks.x: Third, planning does half the work. Attaching instructions to the /plan command gets Copilot to scan the codebase and map out an implementation path before writing a single line of code. Describe the feature or fix in as much detail as possible, then tell it to investigate and come back with questions — edge cases surface in that back-and-forth. Only after the broad strokes are set — which existing systems to use, which classes and methods to create — do you let it write code.

blocks.cap: The input field requesting an implementation plan with the /plan command.

blocks.x: Fourth, don't skip code review. “AI-written code needs review. Even more so if it's code that's going to stay in the project long-term.” When an implementation comes back, read it like a pull request. Select the code and get an explanation with /Explain, or have it critique the code it just wrote with /Review, then attach inline comments to the diff and send it back as a batch. That habit protects code quality and builds a deeper understanding of the system.

blocks.cap: The screen getting an explanation of selected code via /explain.

blocks.x: Fifth, use AI as a personal tutor. To finally tackle shader study she'd long put off, Haffner built a Unity Shader Graph agent tuned toward teaching, and worked on a ground-targeting overlay for combat. For the first two shaders, she worked through nodes and formulas with guidance; for the third, she built it alone but asked for hints instead of answers whenever she got stuck. “By the end, I actually understood what I had built.”

Epic Games has handed off ArtStation and Sketchfab, the 3D art and game asset platforms it bought in 2021, to KitBash3D, an asset-library company. The sale price wasn't disclosed. Among ArtStation's 10 million registered users, those speaking up are welcoming the news. One user wrote that they now have hope the platform will regain its “old glory” and “clear out all the AI flooding the marketplace.”

blocks.cap: Image: Epic Games / ArtStation

blocks.x: As Creative Bloq noted, Epic Games, KitBash3D, and ArtStation each announced the sale separately on August 10. Epic's post put its weight on continuing to prioritize “Unreal Engine 6, Fortnite, the developer ecosystem, and the Epic Games Store,” while ArtStation's post focused on how the sale affects users.

"As of today, ArtStation and Sketchfab are becoming part of KitBash, the company behind the 3D art platform KitBash3D and Greyscalegorilla," ArtStation's statement reads. "With the addition of ArtStation and Sketchfab's art-publishing and discovery platforms, artists will be supported through the full process of turning ideas into form, sharing their work, and building a career. Nothing changes about how creators use ArtStation and Sketchfab. Your portfolios, libraries, and core workflows continue running exactly as they are."

"We deeply care about supporting professional artists, and the time, craft, and effort that goes into that work. Your voice plays an important part in shaping what comes next. Keep sharing it. We're here, and we're listening." That's from a post ArtStation's official account put up on August 11.

Ever since Epic acquired the two platforms in 2021, artists have complained that AI art and assets have been "plastered everywhere, burying real people's work, and routinely used to deceive potential clients."

Artists on the r/ArtStation subreddit are also optimistic about what comes after the sale. "Free from Epic and their love of AI slop. Hope it's good news," one user commented. "I don't trust Epic Games. They genuinely have a talent for ruining everything they touch," another user wrote. "I'm really happy my two favorite websites are no longer in their grip."

Not entirely unrelated to the platform leaving Epic's hands, ArtStation followed up its official statement with another post on X, saying it's "excited to see what the next chapter looks like" and that it's "listening" to user feedback. "There's trust to earn, a lot to learn, and important work ahead. The feedback we hear from artists matters."

Unity and Unreal have held a long grip on development. About 70% of games released on Steam in 2025 were built with these two. Godot has grown sharply in recent years, and some studios run their own engines, like Capcom's RE Engine, but the engine market is effectively split between two names.

Immens founders Arjan Brussee, Sjoerd De Jong, and Michal Valient see room for a new engine in between. Their résumés run through Epic Games, the maker of Unreal, as well as Guerrilla Games, Boss Key, and Apple.

blocks.cap: Arjan Brussee | Image courtesy of Immens

blocks.x: Brussee told GamesIndustry.biz that “there's an opportunity now that didn't exist a few years ago.” “With the help of AI-assisted programming, you can probably start from scratch again. With enough guidance and control, you can build something that quickly has full functionality.”

CTO Valient is adamant that this is a different story from the usual AI talk — this isn't an engine you summon things from with a prompt. “Immens's AI is about building the engine to actually be extensible. The good part is that AI reasons very well about huge amounts of data and codebases. If you design the codebase with that in mind, small teams or individuals can come in and extend the engine.”

Half the reason for building a new engine is today's market. Brussee describes the situation as “brutal.” “It's genuinely hard to succeed with a game. Production costs keep climbing. Something has to change to break that cycle. Is there a way to build with fewer people, in less time, on a smaller budget?”

blocks.cap: Sjoerd De Jong | Image courtesy of Immens

blocks.x: CPO De Jong agrees that standardization and consolidation in the engine market did build a solid foundation. But what's needed now is different. “The industry is facing multiple problems, and continuing as before won't work. What's needed isn't standardization — it's innovation.” He also points to the problem of existing engines being locked into monolithic blocks, forcing developers to bend themselves to fit the software.

Valient also knows AI's weak spot: it's powerful, but “if you're not careful, it can go off the rails fast.” That's why he says Immens is built so users can know what the engine is doing, how it got there, and reproduce that same result again.

blocks.cap: Michal Valient | Image courtesy of Immens

blocks.x: Immens stands on open standards. “If a file is text-based, we can read it,” Brussee said. The goal is to let anything plug in — Blender, Maya, generative tools, or their own tools — without friction.

Funding hasn't been announced yet, and the company has only secured “first commitments.” The company stays deliberately small, just the three founders plus a handful of helpers. “Too much money is also a risk for a startup,” Brussee laughed. A proof of concept showing a flow for editing something with generative AI is targeted for release this month — a schedule that started in April aiming for around year-end, so it's moving twice as fast as expected.

blocks.cap: Astro Bot

blocks.x: Using AI in creative fields has remained uncomfortable. Analysts expect that as AI-made content grows, people will increasingly seek out what feels authentic and human-made. Sony CEO and devoted Oasis fan Hiroki Totoki shares that view. AI can “elevate” creativity, he says, but what draws people to film, music and games is ultimately the human element.
“AI cannot replace that. AI can elevate human creativity.” Totoki said this to the Wall Street Journal. “It really comes down to us. Either we make use of AI, or we get threatened by it.”

Totoki sees AI as a tool. Other creators in the games industry push back even on that. Nobuo Uematsu, the composer known for Final Fantasy music, said AI could help with transitions between sounds in game music, but he has no interest in using generative AI to write new pieces. “I still think it's more rewarding to go through the trouble of making something myself.”
Troy Baker, an active voice actor in games, added his view on the topic. AI can produce content, he said, but not art, because it has no human experience to draw on.
Meanwhile, games like Mecha Chameleon are cited as the opposite of AI slop, thanks to works that foreground and embrace the imperfections of human-made craft.

In Asia, adoption of generative AI is actually rising. A survey by the organization that runs the Tokyo Game Show found that more than 50% of Japanese game developers are incorporating AI into production. By contrast, 50% of developers surveyed at GDC said generative AI is harming the games industry.

When studios disclose their use of AI, the reaction has generally been cold. Crystal Dynamics, developer of Tomb Raider: Legacy of Atlantis, said character designs including Lara Croft are 100% human-made, with AI used only for early concept art and placeholder assets. Sony also said it used machine-learning algorithms on Marvel's Spider-Man 2 as one experiment to speed up development.

Recorded as a session at Unreal Fest Chicago 2026, Duality AI introduced a “vibe simulation” that runs on top of Unreal Engine. The question is simple: what if useful, accurate synthetic data were just a prompt away?

Simulation is a hard tool to do without when building physical AI systems. It speeds up training, allows risk-free testing, and systematically surfaces edge cases. Simulation already holds a broad place in the field.

The problem is that it takes a lot of effort. Simulation work only gets started once you can handle 3D tools, and even small tweaks go through slow, cumbersome procedures. Changing a single scene can take days.

On the other side stands the generative world model. It is intuitive and flexible, but has no grounding in physics. It offers no guarantee that the same conditions produce the same results, and no means of controlling it as desired. Both of those are exactly what training and validation need.

Vibe simulation is an attempt to bring the two together, carrying over the intuition and flexibility of generative world models while holding on to the accuracy, determinism, and physical grounding that simulation has maintained.

Users adjust scenarios through natural-language prompts and an agent interface. At the same time, they retain the precise control needed to inspect, validate, and repeatedly run the AI inside a digital twin environment.

The presenter is Duality AI CEO Apurva Shah, who walks through implementation details alongside a live demo, pointing to the moment static simulation turns into a decision-making and data tool that anyone in an organization can use.
The video was posted to the Unreal Engine channel on August 18, 2026, and runs 48 minutes. More on simulation use cases is available at unrealengine.com/uses/simulation.

blocks.cap: Image credit: ALIVE Inc.

blocks.x: Vapor World: Over the Mind is a new soulslike platformer built around a twisted world and Sekiro-style combat. But all the buzz is about its ugly AI cutscenes, and the director himself is one of the people talking about it.

It built anticipation by passing 100,000 Steam wishlists. What soulslike fans were waiting for was effectively a 2D Lies of P. It launched in early access on Tuesday, August 18, and user reviews sit at 25% positive. Many reviews cite the generative AI disclosed on the Steam page. Developer ALIVE Inc explained that it used AI for voice and cutscenes, but not for “real-time” generation during play.
The disclosure reads: “All content involving AI was produced and reviewed by the team during development, and ships in a fixed, pre-rendered form.”
That review missed things here and there. One Steam reviewer wrote: “This game is so blatantly AI that it ruins the experience outright. AI voices, AI cutscenes, not even a pretense of hiding it.”

In a new Steam post, director Young Kim acknowledged leaning heavily on AI and said he misjudged the scale of the backlash. “If someone asks how I feel about using AI, honestly I'd need to think for a long time before answering. I chose AI because I believed it could reach expression beyond what our current resources allow, and I thought that would let us focus more on the game itself, beyond story and cinematics.”

Several developers have already pushed back on the idea that small teams need generative AI to reach a certain scale or polish. Games have been made well without it all along. Dozens of indie developers who spoke with GamesRadar+ also said they avoid generative AI.

“It was a hasty call,” Kim continued. “Until AI goes one step further, to a point where no one can tell the difference, what I believed was closer to an ideal than to reality. I expected some people would be disappointed by our use of AI. I didn't expect it to grow this big.”

Whether more convincing AI output would solve the problem is unclear, but that isn't the plan for Vapor World either way. “From this point on, we won't use AI-made cutscenes. Not for any cutscene,” Kim promised. “Second, we'll remove all AI cutscenes entirely and replace them completely with originals made by our own hands.”

According to Kim, Vapor World originally used “cutscenes made entirely by our own hands.” But “the results were disastrous every time,” he said. Judging that the team couldn't pull it off themselves, they “turned to AI.” “If that choice hurt your experience, the fault lies not with the tool. It lies with our own shortcomings.”

A surprising admission followed. Kim said “every cutscene in this game was originally made entirely as in-game cutscenes,” and that the team “only recently started replacing them with AI cutscenes.” “What you're seeing now is in the middle of that replacement. So if it looks like no effort went into it, reading it that way based on what's on screen is fair. Looking back, that replacement was the wrong call. At the same time, that's exactly why it can be fixed quickly — the in-game version already exists.” Kim's close: the replacement starts immediately and will be done by the weekend.

Neverness to Everness, the gacha game that launched in 2026, got dragged online without mercy last April over how much of its asset work looked AI-tinged. This is already the third time this year that this game from developer Hotta Games has been caught up in a generative-AI controversy — less than four months after the developers said the game was "built on human creativity" and that they would deliver "the quality players deserve."

blocks.cap: © Hotta Games

blocks.x: Here's what that "quality" looks like: a single AI-made piece of seahorse art, included in the 1.3 update that launched in China on August 12.

There's a worse part. Users on Bilibili, China's livestreaming and social media platform, pointed out that the art looked like it had been made with the free version of ByteDance's AI chatbot, Doubao. How did they figure that out? Did someone run AI-detection software?
No. The answer is far more mundane. The Doubao AI watermark was left sitting right there on the seahorse asset in the 1.3 update. Someone at Hotta Games forgot to remove it.
The global rollout of the 1.3 update is August 19, which is why Chinese players spotted it first — NTE's updates land in China a week earlier.

To be fair, Hotta Games never said, after either the first or the second time it got caught, that it would stop using AI-generated assets. It only said that "AI-assisted tools were used for a small number of background and environment assets" and not for "the characters or story that define this game."

A seahorse asset is hard to call something that defines the game, so that part isn't worth picking apart. Still, it's hard not to wonder whether this really deserved to be handled this carelessly — for a game that made over $200 million within two months of launch, and apparently couldn't be bothered to pay for the paid version of Doubao AI.

The Witcher 3 has a lot to see, and just as much that got cut from Geralt's journey before it shipped. One of those was a system meant to show NPCs reacting in fear of something — it ended up on the cutting-room floor because people, well, started throwing their babies.

blocks.cap: Image courtesy of CD Projekt Red

blocks.x: The Witcher 3's quest designer, Philipp Weber, laid out what happened to Edge magazine. "Because we centered the countryside, players found it easier to get curious."

"If a village only has eight houses, people want to check whether the residents inside are actually real or fake. These days a lot of people care about that kind of detail, and that really gave us trouble."

Scripting the routines and movement of a small countryside village wouldn't be hard in 2026, but in 2012 it was a big deal. "We focused more on faithfully simulating the villagers' day-and-night cycle. The part where they actually reacted to the player wasn't nearly as tight."

Instead of giving each individual a unique routine, they had NPCs cycle through a set of fixed activities — chopping wood, then going inside to eat, or walking somewhere else. That made the village look bustling and kept NPCs from clumping in one spot. "For example, we built 200 spots for the 50 sailors at the Novigrad harbor, so there would still be somewhere to go even if all 50 moved at once," Weber said.

The trouble started when they made these NPCs afraid of something. "NPCs were supposed to have a fear response — drop what they were doing, let go of whatever they were holding, and run off scared. The problem was that one of the 'activities' mothers could be doing was holding and soothing a baby. For weeks, women were dropping babies everywhere."

It was oddly funny, but not the tone CD Projekt Red was going for. So they pulled it out entirely. It's hard not to imagine what it must have been like when the developers saw that scene while playing it themselves. Personally, I think it would've been fine to just leave it in and see what players and reviewers noticed. The Continent could use a bit more laughter.

Some may remember the Join Us trailer that showed up at the Xbox Showcase in June — a dark, funny co-op cult simulator where robed followers ride pigs, spray machine-gun fire, and the whole thing ends with Cthulhu-sized tentacles. The snake gun, though, wasn't in the trailer, says Joe Dietsch, CEO and creative director of developer Wolf Haus Games.

blocks.cap: Joe Dietsch | Image courtesy of Wolf Haus Games

blocks.x: "It was an idea from one of our team member's sons. He said, 'Can't we have a gun that shoots snakes?' We happened to have a tool that scales guns really fast, so we went in and made a snake-shooting gun in about 30 minutes. It was a huge deal for the kid. It's still in the game."

COO Michael Abbott said, "We wanted to shake things up." "We said, 'You don't need a hundred people, twelve can do it,' and everyone didn't believe it — they thought it was impossible." The team comes from the indie film world, where they'd built big things on little money. After 80 pitches, they landed equity investment from Krafton and Lifelike Capital.

What stands out about Join Us is how it's being made. There are only 13 full-time employees. Dietsch said they spent a long time building tools first, early in development. "If a game has one system, that system needs to be something one person can extend and debug. You have to put time into the toolkit so that when a feature later spreads across the whole open-world map, the project doesn't collapse under its own weight."

blocks.cap: The co-op survival game is targeting a release next year

blocks.x: Any mention of a small team usually sets off generative-AI alarms. Dietsch's answer is short. "The short answer is, we don't use generative AI at all. We believe games need a human touch. We love making games, and if we handed development over to agents, there'd be no reason left to get up in the morning and do this."

CFO and narrative director Dooma Wendschuh added, "The slightly longer answer is, we do have a few generative AI subscriptions. We use them for managing schedules and writing email replies. We don't use it at all on the creative side of making the game."

The interesting part is Krafton. It's a company that redefined itself as an "AI-first company" last year, yet it opposed bringing generative AI into Wolf Haus's creative process. "As an investor in our studio, they wanted to make it clear they weren't investing in a studio that makes games with generative AI," Wendschuh said.

blocks.cap: You wouldn't guess the team's size just from the scale of the game world

blocks.x: "We're all creators, and we respect the work of people who create. We really hate the idea that generative AI could take jobs away from voice actors or artists." Dietsch says the 6-kilometer map in Join Us was built entirely by hand, and all 15,000 lines of voiced dialogue in the game were recorded by human actors. "Even for a very small indie game, that mattered a lot to us."

Dietsch, who came from film, says his favorite thing about games is their immediacy. In film, you write an idea on paper and wait two, three, five years for someone to greenlight a shoot. In games, you can take what occurred to you that morning and put it straight into the engine to feel it out by hand.

blocks.cap: Image credit: Eurogamer

blocks.x: Gunz the Duel, the cult-classic third-person action game that first launched in 2006, has returned to Steam. It's a long-awaited comeback for a game that defined a genre, but technical problems and allegations of AI use have cast a shadow over it.

Gunz the Duel was originally made by MAIET Entertainment. The work of bringing it to modern platforms fell to Masangsoft. This revival project was in the works for years, and anticipation built up naturally among old-school PC gamers who remember Gunz.

That anticipation met reality when the game went live on Steam over the weekend. Criticism piled on all at once. First, reports keep coming in that the game is suffering from significant technical problems.

"Masangsoft is a collective of talented people. Not only did they manage to break a 20-year-old game, they keep finding new ways to make it worse." That's from a post by user Fizzion, who also said in-game events and gifts aren't working properly and that the beloved feel of play itself no longer matches the original. "When you slash a blocking enemy, even accounting for angle, there's almost no stagger, and consistency has dropped sharply."

There are also claims that generative AI was used throughout the game. The Gunz the Duel Steam page carries no generative AI disclosure. Another player, EclipseRT, wrote: "From the blatant AI use everywhere in this game, to a developer that won't even follow Steam's own guidelines on disclosing AI use, to unfixed NAT connection issues pushing match pings past 2000, to beta bugs reappearing, to a dev team that's gone completely silent while ignoring all player feedback. Not one person has said a word on Discord in the past year. People have started calling the developers themselves AI at this point. Honestly, you can't even blame them."

Things look similar outside of Steam. The Gunz the Duel subreddit, a hub for fans for more than a decade, is full of complaints. Hackers are visible in-game. Standing still and taking no damage. Posts also keep pointing to a flat UI, network problems, and "AI slop."

Not everyone is having a bad time, of course. Some players are shrugging off the rough edges, happy just to reunite with an old friend. The game also went through a round of server maintenance to address the network issues mentioned above. Some of the worst problems may get resolved with time.
Still, it's a rough start for Gunz. The hope is just that Masangsoft can turn the ship around at least somewhat — or at the very least, get wall air-dashing working again.

blocks.cap: James Pond Legacy: The Pond is Not Enough

blocks.x: It's a good time to be a retro game fan these days. Collections keep pouring out, and now it's finally James Pond fans' turn. Developer System 3 announced the James Pond Legacy: The Pond is Not Enough collection. But the reveal trailer got dragged into accusations that it used generative AI art and assets. As comments pointing out telltale signs of AI imagery piled up fast, System 3 briefly closed public comments on YouTube. Even so, the company didn't budge from its position that no AI was used in the trailer.

At a glance, it's reasonable to suspect generative AI went into the key art and character renders. Every James Pond character carries that smooth, big-eyed look common to AI image generation, layered with a color grade that looks like several yellow filters stacked on top of each other. That's often the result of preference tuning. Models like ChatGPT or DALL-E tend to default to a 'golden hour' color tone, because they're trained on huge amounts of yellow-tinted old paintings, old photographs, and stylized illustrations.
GameSpot asked System 3 for its position. The response flatly denied the allegation that generative AI was used on the characters.

"System 3 has confirmed [with the PR team] that no generative AI was used whatsoever in the creation of the character artwork called out in the trailer. The Pondverse characters were made through a human-led process that started from the original James Pond pixel graphics."

Documentation and images laying out the production process came along with that statement. The sequence starts from the pixel art original, gets redrawn in Illustrator and Photoshop, goes through a 3D render, and then gets touched up once more in Photoshop. Comments on the trailer were later reopened, and the developer posted a blog entry explaining the process.

This isn't the first time James Pond has brushed up against generative AI. The legacy sequel James Pond: Rogue AI was harshly criticized by original creator Chris Sorrell for using the technology. "I hate almost everything they're doing with a passion." That's what Sorrell told Time Extension in an interview last year.

The collection packages James Pond: Underwater Agent, James Pond 2: Robocod, James Pond 3: Operation Starfish, and The Aquatic Games Starring James Pond and the Aquabats. It launches in October 2026 as a Switch 2 exclusive. It also includes an interactive history archive collecting the original's hand-drawn artwork. That artwork is much better.

Generative AI remains a hot-button issue in game development, especially when it's used for art assets. Companies keep repeating the explanation that it was placeholder material before being swapped for hand-made art. Pearl Abyss and Sandfall Interactive have both said this.

Larian CEO Swen Vincke has said before that his studio used generative AI tools to explore new game ideas, concept art, and placeholder text. A retraction and clarification followed almost immediately. Others have drawn the opposite line. Mega Crit, developer of Slay the Spire 2, said it would rather pick a "messier" drawing over one a machine churned out when conceiving a game.

Kim Yong-ha, head of the IO Division at NEXON Games, took the stage for the first session on day one of BIC2026, the keynote. The talk was titled 'How Does a Game Become a “World”?' The organizers had asked for a keynote connecting subculture, IP, and indie games, and after turning that over, the word he landed on was “world.” The talk itself unfolded in three parts, following those three words.

blocks.cap: This year's BIC lineup, with Kim Yong-ha's talk as the very first session on day one.

blocks.x: Part one looked at how far the subculture market has come. Blue Archive now draws about 4,000 people to its offline running events, and Pixiv-related submissions have passed 270,000. Sales at AK PLAZA in Hongdae have grown to roughly three times their 2021 level. “Subculture may have been a small niche in the past,” he said. “But I think the subculture market as a whole may now be bigger than any single major game.”

Part two was about IP. Beyond logos, settings, characters, and story, he argued that in games, “gameplay itself” often forms the IP. The three pillars that stick in memory are repeated actions, memorable symbols, and relationships. Pokémon has capturing and battling, the Monster Ball, trainers and Pokémon; PUBG has dropping in and surviving, helmets, squads. Blue Archive started from “academy,” “youth,” and “military,” cast the player as a “teacher,” and pulled the tablet — its interaction device — down into the entire UI.

Part three was AI. When his division held an internal game jam, it produced 48 playable games in just two days from that one division alone. Most of the work happened within regular working hours, so the actual production time was around 10 hours each. Last year, roughly 20,000 games were released on Steam, and about half of them — around 10,000 — have fewer than 10 reviews.

blocks.cap: The number everyone in the industry keeps repeating these days: “around 20,000 games went up on Steam in the past year.”

blocks.x: Kim Yong-ha summed up AI's strengths as two things: the ability to find correct answers, and the ability to reproduce specific patterns when there's enough training data. But questions like “mul-naengmyeon or bibim-naengmyeon” or “older-sister type or younger-sister type” have no correct answer to begin with. An AI with no self to call its own, and no taste, can't answer these.

That's why taste belongs to people, and so does the process of raising taste into an eye for aesthetics. He gave his own experience as an example: he loved characters with glasses so much that he filled a cast entirely with glasses-wearing characters, and got panned for it. Ask an AI why everyone hates glasses and you'll get a plausible-sounding answer. But only he himself can dig into “why do I, who love glasses, love glasses.”

blocks.cap: The line Kim Yong-ha kept pushing throughout was “build your own taste.”

blocks.x: Make, compare, explain why, and choose again. That repetition is what builds an eye for aesthetics. “AI can explain things,” he said. “But AI is a being that ‘learned to cook from text alone,’ so it can't actually taste the food.” The same goes for indies. The creator of one recently hit indie game had already made 43 others before it.

Meta's experimental vibe-coding game app Pocket is rolling out across the US. It's the same app that quietly launched last month in Brazil, its test market. Make a small, interactive game with an AI prompt, and it lands in a scrollable feed.

blocks.cap: Image credit: Meta, image modified with AI

blocks.x: Behind it is an acquisition from earlier this year, when Meta brought over the entire team behind the vibe-coding game platform Gizmo. These interactive experiences, which Meta calls “Gizmos,” respond to touch and phone tilt, play sound effects, and can include clips of your favorite songs.
They can also use photos from the camera roll or access the camera itself. Once a game is finished, posting it to a profile lets others save it, remix it into something different, or repost it as-is.

blocks.cap: Pocket. Image credit: Meta

blocks.x: It's the latest move in a push to bring AI creation tools into the mainstream. Meta had already let people make AI images with the Meta AI app and AI videos with its experimental app Vibes. On the July earnings call, Mark Zuckerberg credited the faster pace of launches to building software with AI. “Earlier this year we shipped Instagram Instants. We also just shipped Forum, a groups-only app, and Seller, a marketplace app. I think it's going to get a lot easier to ship new apps.”

Beyond Instants, Forum, and Seller, Meta has also put out an experimental AI-generated bedtime stories feature, and this week shipped a Meta AI app for Mac. With Pocket launching, the original app it acquired from Atma Sciences, Gizmo, is shutting down.

blocks.cap: © Sony

blocks.x: A new Sony AI game patent application has surfaced online. It describes technology where an agent trained on player data plays a game in a person's place. If an authorized bot can grind it out for you, is there any reason to earn experience yourself? There's a more unsettling part, though. The patent even describes the possibility of players buying and selling their own training data with each other for real money.

Sony's patent No. 19138338, found by Cheat Happens, was filed in 2022 and only became publicly available on July 23 of last month. It covers "technology for creating an agent that plays a game on a user's behalf." Some may remember a similar Sony patent published this past January, the one describing an AI-controlled "ghost" that finishes a game for you — but this one goes much further into Black Mirror territory.

While the earlier patent said the AI was trained on gameplay footage, the AI in patent 19138338 learns a user's actual playing habits. Patent drawing 11 shows that this AI can be instructed to carry out tasks like "gathering money," "advancing the story," or "boss battles" without any user input.

The truly strange part comes next. The patent states that when another user's data is used to create User A's agent, game system 1 can be set up to charge User A for that use. For example, if User A creates an agent using a famous player's data, the system could allow them to purchase that data.

If you buy a pro player's AI data and watch that AI finish the entire game, how is that different from watching gameplay footage on YouTube? Buying a game, then buying a "famous player's" AI version to finish it for you — that's not a video game, that's just a video.

Game companies file patents on all sorts of technologies and design principles all the time; that doesn't mean they intend to actually build them. Still, even if Sony never makes an AI player agent official, there's no guarantee some other company won't try something similar and start selling it.
Unreal MCP now works in UEFN, the Unreal Editor for Fortnite. In the video, UEFN evangelist Magnus Enebakk walks through UEFN's Model Context Protocol (MCP) step by step.

What it shows is how agentic coding tools like Claude Code or Cursor work together inside the editor. It goes as far as writing and compiling Verse, placing devices and setting them up, and running a play session to check the results.

According to the Epic documentation linked in the video, UEFN MCP works by running an MCP server inside the editor and connecting over local HTTP. It exposes tools for reading, editing, and compiling Verse source, manipulating entities and components in the scene graph, placing creative devices and setting their properties, and starting, stopping, and checking the status of play sessions. The default address is http://127.0.0.1:8000/mcp.

To use it, turn on Python Editor Scripting and UEFN MCP Toolsets in the project settings, place a .mcp.json in the project root, and run your agent from that folder. The clients named in the documentation are Claude Code, Cursor, and MCP Inspector.
The new Unity CLI package turns the editor into a local server. Once the editor exposes an API, a terminal, an agent, or a custom-built interface can all send commands into it to run.

The CLI itself is a standalone executable you install separately. On the Unity CLI documentation page, copy the install command for your system, paste it into a terminal, and run it. Then add the Pipeline package to your project. That's the package that runs inside the editor and connects it to the CLI.

Once the package is in, the CLI attaches to the running editor and pulls up the list of commands the project has. Play mode, status checks, recompiling, and running tests are all on that list, and it works with any agent with no extra setup.

There's also eval. It runs C# directly inside a live Unity instance — the editor or a running build — to handle one-off tasks. That's how the video wraps up: until now, the Unity editor was the only way in, but now it's open to whatever tool fits the moment.

Video has run on adaptive streaming for a long time. One source file reaches any screen, any connection, and playback starts with almost no wait. Miris moved that approach to 3D. 80 Level asked Miris CTO Sean Looper what spatial streaming changes for developers.

Looper started in animation and visual effects. He led real-time streaming graphics and HPC teams at DreamWorks Animation and also passed through Sony Pictures Imageworks, working on more than 60 films along the way. He later built HPC products for real-time graphics processing at thousands-of-CPU scale at AWS, and started working with Miris about three years ago.

3D delivery has always been a tradeoff. Pre-rendering like a film gives the best image quality but locks the viewpoint; game engines move freely but cut image quality. Pixel streaming, which rents cloud GPUs, loads on new burdens of GPU supply, cost, and latency. Looper says the industry has treated this tradeoff like a law of physics. That premise broke once AI pushed the computation burden to the front end.

blocks.cap: Miris brand image — 3D streaming without limits

blocks.x: When a customer hands over the highest-quality original asset, AI optimization runs for anywhere from minutes to hours depending on the asset and settings. The result is, in effect, a single spatial database. From there, a smart client reads device performance, network conditions, the viewing point of the content, and the nature of the asset, and pulls in only exactly what's needed.

The use case getting the biggest response right now is asset review. Distributed teams check the original, with lighting, materials, and dense geometry left intact, on a tablet, an iPhone, or a low-spec laptop. Medical visualization, media and entertainment, e-commerce, and industrial digital twins face the same problem. The SDK is up on GitHub, and it drops in with a few lines of TypeScript or plain HTML.

blocks.cap: Miris CTO Sean Looper

blocks.x: Looper sees 3D following the same path the internet took from image-centric to video-centric, with generative AI pulling that speed forward sharply. Just as smartphone cameras opened up video production, people who couldn't handle professional software are now making 3D.

Neksseosseu (CEO Jang Hyun-guk) announced on the 19th that it had opened 'Neksseosseu AI Labs,' a portal gathering 11 AI solutions it developed in-house. The portal was built to take AI research results beyond demos and prove them out as commercial products ready for immediate use in real work.

blocks.cap: Neksseosseu unveils 'AI Labs' portal gathering 11 AI solutions

blocks.x: The released solutions were built with the autonomous development platform 'Neksseosseu AI Framework.' Enter a goal, and 33 AI agents and 39 specialized functions collaborate to automatically carry out the entire process from planning through design, development, and verification. It's a structure that produces polished products without a person writing code directly.

The solutions registered on the portal are split into three areas: content creation, work automation, and blockchain integration. The content area includes the 3D model creation tool 'Text to 3D,' the ad trailer creation solution 'Eibeu,' and the pixel-art generator 'Perfect Pixel.' The work automation area is made up of the marketing platform 'Kiroro,' the automatic meeting-minutes solution 'Bap,' and 'ImageToApp,' which turns plans into apps.

In the blockchain integration area, it unveiled 'OneChain Skill,' built on natural-language commands. This solution had its safety proven last June when it passed every item of the AI skill security inspection run by CertiK, the global Web3 security firm. Along with these, the text-based game creation tool 'wasd,' the AI video solution 'Red Studio,' and 'StoryMaker' round out the 11 solutions on offer.

Neksseosseu CEO Jang Hyun-guk said, "One of the keys to the era of AI transition is how fast you can prove technology research as a product that can be demonstrated in reality," adding, "We're already implementing products at the speed of thought through AI, and we plan to expand that capability across our blockchain platform business as a whole."

Roblox is open-sourcing three of its AI safety models through ROOST (Robust Open Online Safety Tools Model Community). ROOST is an independent nonprofit that builds and maintains open-source infrastructure for online safety, founded by Roblox together with Google, OpenAI, and Discord in 2025.

blocks.cap: Image source: Roblox

blocks.x: The models being released are the PII classifier, Roblox Sentinel, and the newest voice safety classifier. All three are already running on the Roblox platform.

The PII classifier catches attempts to share or request personally identifiable information, filtering even cases where spelling is twisted, slang is used, or another platform is referenced indirectly. Roblox is also releasing an evaluation dataset for this tool: "synthetic samples of English-language multi-user chat" modeled on common tricks used to dodge PII filters.

Roblox Sentinel detects early signs that a child is at risk. The newest voice safety classifier moderates voice chat in real time and incorporates feedback from the ROOST community. Roblox is also releasing a new evaluation dataset so other companies can benchmark their own safety tools. The latest version covers 30 languages and eight violation types.

Naren Koneru, vice president of trust and safety engineering, said, "Sharing these models gives other platforms a solid starting point to train and refine their own moderation tools," adding, "We hope that when they share their results, we get something back too, from that learning and feedback." He added that safety is a shared responsibility that no single company can solve alone.

Earlier this week, the U.S. Senate Judiciary Committee's crime and counterterrorism subcommittee said it had opened an investigation, saying Roblox appears to prioritize revenue and engagement metrics over child safety. Roblox must turn over materials on child safety, sexual and physical abuse, bullying, and financial exploitation by August 31, 2026. In recent years, Roblox has rolled out a string of measures, including restricting direct messages for users under 13, facial-recognition age verification worldwide, 'sensitive topics' content tags, and tightened moderation policies.

blocks.cap: The free Blender addon Spider Walker

blocks.x: Roman 'Iltaen' Gibadulin, an artist known for low-poly 3D work, released a free addon for Blender 5.2 LTS. It moves the legs of a multi-legged rig, spider-style, procedurally and in real time.

Here's how it works: each leg raycasts toward the floor and plants its foot one after another as the character moves. It even reads the direction of travel ahead of time, so legs land out in front instead of trailing behind the body. If the motion looks good, the built-in bake feature can turn the real-time simulation into a regular keyframed action for further tweaking.

To use it, you need an armature with a body (root) bone and independent leg controller bones that aren't parented to the body bone. You also need a collection of mesh objects for the feet to walk on. Since Spider Walker ultimately just calculates each foot's next footstep position, there's room for it to work on bipedal or quadrupedal rigs too.

The creator describes what happens every frame like this: it reads the center bone's current world coordinates to estimate the body's velocity, then checks each leg's current planted position against a predicted target. The target is the body-relative rest position pushed forward in the direction of travel, scaled to velocity. Once a leg strays far enough from that target, it raycasts downward from the predicted point to find a landing spot and starts a step. The foot lifts, arcs, and comes down on the new target. Legs move one at a time in list order, so you won't get all legs stepping at once.

The creator said part of the code was built and refined with AI's help. 80 Level also recommends Lincoln Magisson's tutorial for anyone who wants to dig deeper into procedural animation for multi-legged creatures.

Luke Plunkett first covered 1666: Amsterdam because the game's reveal trailer had AI-generated images mixed into it. The subject of this piece, which he hopes will be the second and last, is that studio co-founder Patrice Désilets seems to have learned nothing from that controversy.

In an interview published in Eurogamer, Désilets tried to explain the AI elements in the reveal trailer. "We live in a world full of AI. Let's be honest with each other. But there were things in the pipeline that we didn't polish enough, and since then we made sure not to use AI anywhere in the game."

Plunkett thinks this answer completely misread the room. Désilets is, he writes, "so steeped in tech, up to his eyeballs in it, that he's trying to wave off a serious, insulting PR disaster with a 'sorry we got caught doing what everyone does' routine."

Désilets' explanation continues like this. "You can ask AI for 75 variations of one subject. But you can't get 75 different illustrators to produce variations in three seconds. That's the world we live in, and we were making the game with a small team, so we put that in."

Plunkett writes that this particular line sticks with him. The game has more than a dozen professional artists attached to it, and gamers' attitudes toward AI use in game development, especially in artwork, are already well documented.

When the Eurogamer interview, conducted in Amsterdam, pressed further on the subject, Désilets was reluctant to say more. The on-the-scene account adds this: "At the time, another outlet's reporter and a creator present said this is just a tool you use, so this kind of discussion isn't necessary."

Plunkett's conclusion is simple. Developers may want to steer interviews toward other topics, but public concern over AI use remains a legitimate question for reporters to pursue. This brief back-and-forth captures, as of 2026, the tension between developers and the games press.

blocks.cap: Luke Dicken and David 'Rez' Graham on the Game Developer podcast

blocks.x: The episode the Game Developer podcast released on August 21, 2026 is titled "We're finally talking about AI, ft. David 'Rez' Graham and Luke Dicken." It means exactly what it says: they're finally talking about AI.

Three people sat down for it. Senior editor Bryant Francis hosts, with David 'Rez' Graham, a former senior engineer at Maxis, and Dr. Luke Dicken, who headed AI at Take-Two, as guests. Both are longtime fixtures in game development.

The conversation starts from how each of them has personally weathered the recent AI frenzy that has swept Silicon Valley. The intro sums it up this way: what they still love about game AI, and how to judge what's actually valuable about artificial intelligence without getting swept up in empty hype, whether you're an AI enthusiast or standing on the other side.

It isn't just technical talk, though. The episode sets technical AI concepts alongside broader questions of what work is and where value comes from in game development. It's also an attempt to draw a line between long-standing game AI design and today's generative tools.

The Game Developer podcast is a biweekly record of game development, hosted by Bryant Francis, edited by Pierre Landriau, with music by Mike Meehan. Recent episodes have covered Godot engine adoption and game localization.

blocks.cap: A banner spanning 15 years of game AI, from retro arcade screens to Go boards, strategy game interfaces and starships

blocks.x: From Atari to Go and then to StarCraft, games have produced several of AI's biggest breakthroughs. Google DeepMind now pairs directly with game developers to prototype new play experiences.
Since it opened its doors in 2010, games have been DeepMind's window into intelligence. Founder Demis Hassabis himself came from a game development background.

It started with a small team training a deep neural network to learn Atari 2600 games from screen pixels alone. The model, called DQN, learned 49 games without game-specific design, and a 2015 Nature paper opened the era of deep reinforcement learning.

Next came more complex games. AlphaGo beat world champion Lee Sae Dol in 2016, and AlphaGo Zero surpassed the earlier version through self-play alone. AlphaZero learned chess, shogi and Go with a single algorithm. In 2019, AlphaStar reached grandmaster level in StarCraft II.

AlphaGo's move 37 was so unfamiliar that commentators mistook it for an error, and it overturned centuries of accumulated Go wisdom. AlphaFold solved the 50-year problem of protein structure prediction, leading to the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

Given enough goals and training, AI conquered any game. But the real world has no scoreboard and no rulebook. Can it understand and handle game worlds the way a person does? That question produced SIMA, the Scalable Instructable Multiworld Agent, which watches the screen, understands natural-language instructions, and acts through keyboard and mouse.

SIMA 2, built on Gemini, is closer to a companion that reasons and converses in real time. It shows human-level play in 3D environments like No Man's Sky, Valheim and Hydroneer. The key point is that it can be attached without touching the game's code. That's what makes possible NPC responses that scripting couldn't produce, and QA for builds that change with every commit.

blocks.cap: A workshop where the Google DeepMind and Fenris Creations teams exchanged playable prototypes and feedback

blocks.x: This time's partner is Fenris Creations, the independent studio behind the EVE Universe. Launched in 2003, EVE Online is a space simulation where thousands of people have shared a single universe for more than 20 years. Real, moving supply and demand, and a trade network linking thousands of star systems, were all built by human hands.

From a research standpoint, the conditions are about as good as it gets. It requires, all at once, the ability to keep learning without forgetting, memory that exceeds a model's context window, planning over years, and multi-agent dynamics tangled up with negotiation and economics.

Hilmar Pétursson, CEO of Fenris Creations, said, "EVE Online was conceived from day one as a player-driven sandbox where consequences last," adding, "with Google DeepMind, we're stepping into uncharted territory where AI has to learn, adapt, and remember."
EVE Vanguard handles fast tactical decisions on the ground in first-person view, and EVE Frontier, with its programmable Smart Assemblies, is an environment where the rules themselves can change.
Some results are already felt by players. Aura Guidance uses Gemini to pass real Rookie Help questions and answers to new pilots. The goal, now as before, is to be a catalyst, not a replacement.

Rainbow Six Siege sharply cut voice chat abuse after adding ToxMod, Modulate's AI voice intelligence platform. Having seen player behavior improve over a year, Ubisoft extended its partnership with Modulate to keep pushing for healthier voice conversations.

The results showed up together across several metrics. After in-game sanctions were introduced, severe voice abuse fell 50%, and overall voice toxicity dropped 30% as well. Within two weeks of turning sanctions on, toxicity per session fell from about 37% to 8%. The platform now analyzes roughly 800,000 hours of voice per month.

Voice moderation is among the trickiest game safety problems there is. Fast-moving tactical play, open-mic team chat, and expressions specific to this one game all pile on top of each other, overwhelming older approaches. Even before ToxMod, the team received reports of harmful voice chat, but had no way to verify incidents or back up sanction decisions consistently.

Lancelot Satge, who leads game protection for Rainbow Six Siege at Ubisoft, said, "ToxMod was a solution we could drop in right away, yet powerful enough to learn our game's language and reality and adapt to it."

The rollout started with a four-week pilot run. During that period, ToxMod analyzed voice in real time but took no action visible to players. In the meantime, the team learned the character of the environment, tuned detection thresholds, and figured out how to tell harmful behavior apart from legitimate tactical callouts. Live operation began in September 2025.

What the analysis revealed is that harmful behavior clusters. In a 34-day assessment, about 35% of users flagged on a given day generated two or more high-severity detections, and that group accounted for about 66% of that day's incidents. That made narrowly targeted intervention possible instead of broad discipline.

The next task is refining operations around player reports and sanction history. The two teams also plan to look at recognizing good behavior, identifying people who give useful callouts and welcome new players. Satge asked, "When someone makes a good callout, helps a teammate, and sets an example, how can we recognize and reward that?"

Modulate CEO Mike Pappas emphasized the ability to read context. "A transcript alone can't reliably tell a tactical callout apart from friendly banter or targeted hate speech." Rainbow Six Siege has more than 100 million registered players, and voice chat is an inseparable part of competitive play.

blocks.cap: The Signal AI benchmark released by Skillprint

blocks.x: Skillprint has opened a beta for the Skillprint Signal Benchmark, the first public benchmark to score how much an AI model actually improves a real person's performance.

Existing benchmarks look at what a model knows, how accurately it answers questions, and how well it completes set tasks. Signal looks at something different. The company explained that it measures how well a model adjusts a live game in real time to move an actual person toward a target mental state, such as deeper focus, relaxation, or improvement in a specific cognitive ability.
