Signal places an AI model inside a game that real participants play. While a person plays, the model adjusts the game's parameters in real time toward a set outcome, such as focus or relaxation. It then measures how much the player's state actually changed, and ranks models based on that outcome.

It's built on six years of research, drawing on more than 500,000 players and more than 1,000 games, quizzes and simulations to examine the relationship between play, cognition, mood and player state.

With this release, Skillprint has entered its next stage. Over six years of building a play-based intelligence platform, it has held onto one belief: AI should augment people's abilities instead of replacing them.

Skillprint CEO Chethan Ramachandran said, "Most AI benchmarks tell you how smart a model is on its own. Drawing on years of decoding human cognition at scale, we built a benchmark that tells you whether that model can actually help a person boost their performance and intelligence. As AI becomes part of everyday life, we think that will be one of the most important measures there is."

blocks.cap: Nvidia ACE coming to Aniimo. Image credit: Pawprint Studio

blocks.x: Alongside the launch of Ray Reconstruction for DLSS 4.5, Nvidia announced it's bringing ACE technology to other games too. That's the same tech that powers PUBG: Battlegrounds' generative AI teammate. This time the stage is Aniimo, an open-world monster-collecting RPG from Chinese developer Pawprint Studio. It follows the "legally distinct" Pokémon formula that games like Palworld have settled into, but with Nvidia's technology layered on, players will actually be able to talk with their monsters.

“In early 2027, Nvidia ACE will run on RTX GPUs, and players will be able to talk naturally with their own Aniimo.” That's what Nvidia senior product marketing manager Ike Nnoli said at a Gamescom pre-briefing that RPS also attended. “You'll have conversations, teach them new skills like crafting or mining, and get to know each one's distinct personality.”
The PUBG AI teammate project is built so NPCs use an AI brain to react to combat situations and pull their weight in tactical maneuvers. Aniimo's version is closer to the more familiar AI chatbot.

During the Q&A, someone asked how they prevent generative AI NPCs from being talked into handing out quest rewards early, something that happened last year in the Chinese RPG Where Winds Meet. Nnoli's answer: “With our technology, developers have full control over how far a character will go in responding to a player — behavior and response guardrails, right down to the model instructions.” Aniimo keeps its scope tied to Homeland, the base where Pawprint has players craft, mine, and gather resources, and the monsters only do set activities there. Reactions are set to come as “specific actions and emojis” rather than voiced dialogue.

Seen that way, Aniimo's use case is closer to an AI version of Nintendogs. That's not surprising as this kind of technology spreads. Still, there's a catch attached: unlike PUBG's AI soldiers, kids are far more likely to be the ones interacting with this AI monster. Here's hoping it's less prone than Fortnite's AI Darth Vader to having its mask slip mid-conversation or getting goaded into mischievous responses.
Nvidia has signaled that ACE technology is coming to Aniimo in early 2027. The Steam page still just says "coming soon," but the game's launch is probably around the same time.

blocks.cap: A scene from the Humankind 2 reveal trailer. Image source: Amplitude Studios

blocks.x: Gamescom 2026 had just begun, and controversy broke out before the Opening Night Live pre-show had even ended. A game's official debut was accused of using AI. Humankind 2 was unveiled with a trailer, but the live-action scenes looked suspiciously like AI, and there was no disclosure on the official YouTube channel or in the video itself.
Right after the trailer dropped, the official Twitter/X account responded, saying no AI was used and that photos of the actors would be shared soon.

Update, 15:00 ET. The official Humankind Twitter/X account issued a statement saying the trailer was shot at Mu Boyana Film Studios in Sofia. Real actors performed with custom-made props on physical sets. The account reaffirmed its promise to release behind-the-scenes photos.

The original Humankind came out in 2021. Given today's market pace, a sequel this soon counts as fast. But anticipation quickly turned into confusion. The reveal trailer's live-action segment drew comments calling it “AI slop,” along with harsher words.
YouTube comments were dominated by talk of AI. Some defended it as genuine live-action, but most were sarcastic, and few comments offered evidence that the trailer had no AI.

Strategy and civilization games like Humankind are remembered for things other than graphics. Yet the first conversation around Humankind 2 wasn't about the game but about alleged AI use in the trailer, and that allegation was quickly reversed. Responding to a deleted post, the official Humankind Twitter/X account confirmed that no AI was used in making the trailer, and said it would show photos of the actors too.

At least the debate over AI use in the trailer settles here. It would be even better if that clarity carried through to the full game. AI remains a hot topic, and the backlash is especially strong in creativity-driven fields like games, which is why Steam game pages are required to disclose AI use. Transparent confirmation like this eases players' concerns.

blocks.cap: Five people weighing in on AI adoption in the Nordic game industry. Image source: PocketGamer.biz

blocks.x: This is the first installment of a series on AI in the Nordic game industry. We spoke with five people close to that change: two studio founders, a co-founder of an AI-native studio, a lawyer specializing in games, and a business development manager who works across several studios.

Mikael Gummerus, chairman and co-founder of Dodreams, whose Drive Ahead! has passed 300 million organic downloads, speaks candidly about how far AI has come into the company. “At Dodreams, the biggest thing AI has changed is data analysis, and turning that data into actionable suggestions. Manual work has dropped a lot, and we use fewer separate systems. We even get insights we didn't have the staff to find before.” Unity development and art haven't seen the same leap yet. Since those areas are hands-on, the gains are gradual.

blocks.cap: From left: Mikael Gummerus of Dodreams, Tatu Petersen-Jessen of Odd Latent. Image source: PocketGamer.biz

blocks.x: Tatu Petersen-Jessen, who previously worked as senior art director at Rovio and art team manager at Remedy, built Odd Latent as an openly AI-native studio. The change he sees isn't a new title but how much scope one person handles. “We call that role a ‘game specialist.’ It's effectively a one-person game team moving between art, design, and code.” What has disappeared isn't individual craft but the narrow job of working in just one discipline and handing off to the next specialist. “I think it's closer to returning to how game development originally worked, before complexity and competition drove up team size and division of labor.”

blocks.cap: From left: Olivia Tunkelo of Brimstone AI, Tuomas Pelkonen of Nordia Law. Image source: PocketGamer.biz

blocks.x: Olivia Tunkelo, COO and co-founder of Brimstone AI, says the company sits in a peculiar spot. “Brimstone is at a unique intersection where adoption and resistance overlap, because it's an AI product for people who are against AI.” Internally, AI-assisted development is used to quickly test expected features, with finishing touches done by hand. She said the goal of keeping human creativity at the center hasn't changed because of AI.

The question itself that reaches Tuomas Pelkonen, a lawyer at Nordia Law, hasn't changed: do you see risk in using AI this way? What has changed is the density of explanation needed and the number of use cases. The question of what the AI Act actually requires of studios also keeps coming up. “Especially in triple-A, players may simply refuse to accept AI-generated content. The older the brand, the deeper the attachment fans have to their favorite games and characters, so they can't stand even the thought that it might have been made with AI.” Also up for discussion is ‘shadow AI,’ where developers secretly use tools the studio hasn't adopted. If someone, pressed by a deadline, touches it alone without disclosing it, the company only finds out after launch — and by then it's both a commercial and a legal problem.

Hind Toufga, who handles business development across several studios, sees adoption maturing quickly. It covers coding assistance, automated testing, QA, localization, data analysis, concept development, and repetitive tasks. “The most interesting part is that AI isn't replacing creative staff — it's letting small teams work faster and freeing developers to spend more time where human creativity and judgment are truly needed.” She said the studios that gain the most aren't the ones using AI the most, but the ones that know where their pipeline actually improves.
This week, at Gamescom in Cologne, Germany, NVIDIA laid out the next steps for RTX gaming: support for new games, anti-cheat technology, and improved image quality.

Electronic Arts, Embark and Ubisoft are bringing flagship titles to NVIDIA RTX Spark, which launches this fall. That follows KRAFTON, NetEase, Riot Games and XBOX, which announced RTX Spark support at COMPUTEX in May.

blocks.cap: NVIDIA RTX Spark, unveiled at Gamescom. Image source: NVIDIA

blocks.x: EA's EA SPORTS F1 25 and Apex Legends, Ubisoft's Anno 117: Pax Romana, and Embark Studios' ARC Raiders and THE FINALS. NVIDIA worked closely with these developers and ecosystem partners to ensure these games, among the most played on PC right now, run smoothly on RTX Spark devices.

“We're excited to bring Anno 117: Pax Romana to a new generation of RTX-based PCs.” That's from Stéphane Jankowski, executive producer at Ubisoft for Anno 117: Pax Romana. “Our team makes this game look expansive — whole districts, long sightlines, thousands of details pouring in all at once. Seeing RTX Spark hold up that level of precision on a single chip is really impressive.”

RTX Spark brings together personal AI agents, advanced content creation, and high-performance gaming on a single platform. It's a device designed from the ground up for the next generation of Windows PCs. For gamers, it means a Windows device with RTX technologies like DLSS and Reflex built in.

Supporting PC gaming today takes more than just getting games running. Many large online games rely on sophisticated anti-cheat technology to keep play fair across platforms. NVIDIA has been working with EA to bring native support for EA Javelin Anticheat to RTX Spark, covering major EA multiplayer titles like EA SPORTS F1 25. RTX Spark launches this fall.

blocks.cap: EA SPORTS F1 25 coming to RTX Spark. Image source: NVIDIA

blocks.x: The Gamescom announcements aren't limited to RTX Spark. DLSS 4.5 Ray Reconstruction opened up starting today, using a second-generation transformer model to further boost image quality in ray- and path-traced scenes. An AI network trained on NVIDIA supercomputers takes the place of traditional denoisers, reconstructing better pixels even in frame areas rays never reached. CONTROL Resonant and 007 First Light are getting path tracing. Gears of War: E-Day adds RTX Mega Geometry. RTX Remix released a major update for the Painkiller RTX mod and is preparing The Elder Scrolls III: Morrowind RTX. GeForce NOW is getting new DLSS 4.5 controls and expanded Steam Machine support.

blocks.cap: Final Fantasy: Crystal Chronicles. Image source: Square Enix

blocks.x: Kumi Tanioka, composer of Final Fantasy: Crystal Chronicles, has spoken out about an album that appeared on Spotify under his name. The issue is simple: he has nothing to do with it.

In a post on X, Tanioka said the situation was confusing. He asked whether the Spotify EP credited to his name, titled A Village Built on Wind, was the work of someone else with the same name, or something made with generative AI. “This album is definitely not something I made.”

Tanioka is a verified Spotify artist, meaning the service has recognized him as an “authentic” creator. Even so, the EP was assigned to his name. There's no sign that he was involved in the registration process.

He isn't the only one confused. Digital Sonic Design, the publisher behind some of his music, also issued a statement. It said the tracks don't infringe on the copyright of Tanioka's work, but the mislabeling could confuse the public. The company also noted that the same tracks are marked as AI-generated on YouTube Music.

The statement closes this way: “This looks like a case that exploits a structural weakness in streaming service platforms. Given past instances where unreleased, unofficial tracks were reproduced by ear and distributed, we're considering some form of response.”

blocks.cap: Dragon Quest 10. Image credit: Square Enix

blocks.x: Yuji Horii, creator of Dragon Quest, said he is a fan of AI. He said AI has advanced noticeably in recent years and now “barely makes things up.” The remark came when he was asked about the Gemini-based chatbot recently added to the series' MMO.

The Dragon Quest series is considered one of the games with one of the earliest AI systems in gaming history. In 1990's Dragon Quest 4, players gave party members rough instructions and AI chose each character's actions. This latest AI addition has not been welcomed nearly as warmly.

Dragon Quest 10, an MMO that runs only in Japan, recently released its seventh and final expansion, Lost Children of Time and Space, and opinions were split over a new feature in it: a companion called Oshaberi Slimey, literally “chatty slime,” the series' iconic blue slime wearing a jester's hat. Fans were disappointed to learn this Slimey runs on a Google Gemini-based chatbot.

In an interview with Famitsu, carried by GamesRadar+, Horii explained why he added Slimey and shared his view of AI. “These days, AI is really smart, so it's fun,” he said. “No matter what you ask it, it barely makes things up now.”

AI often runs into trouble with factual accuracy, since it tends to give an answer even when it lacks the needed information. This game designer, synonymous with Square Enix, has had the same experience. “A while back I asked AI about myself, and it told me I was a 'Nintendo employee,'” he said, laughing.
Still, he defended AI this way: “AI is evolving, and these days there's a lot you can do with it. Since Slimey is someone to talk to, I think it lowers the barrier to engaging with AI.”

IRONMACE, maker of Dark and Darker, has shared how it used Aura. A designer with no technical background touched the game's codebase directly, prototyped a tutorial system, and worked with engineers, finishing in just a few weeks what the studio estimated would take 5-6 weeks.

Using AI in game development goes well beyond generative art, and some studios are already testing new techniques outside the spotlight. For IRONMACE, that meant seeing whether a designer with little programming experience could directly contribute to implementing a major new feature with the AI coding assistant Aura.

The test subject was something Dark and Darker notably lacked: a proper tutorial. Its absence had been explained away by the extraction dungeon crawler's “hardcore” identity, but the real obstacle was development resources. Building a tutorial would have meant pulling developers off urgent work to focus on new-player onboarding.

blocks.cap: Dark and Darker. Image credit: IRONMACE

blocks.x: In the words of IRONMACE CEO and co-founder Terence Park: “My background is in game design and production. I dabble in scripting and know data structures, but programming isn't my strength.” Normally, this would have meant assembling a dedicated team with staff for each role, more meetings, and managing an unwieldy pipeline.

In practice, things stayed flexible. The initial meeting sketched out the idea, after which Park made the big decisions and filled in the detailed context with Aura. Once the team decided on a checkpoint-style tutorial, Park built each checkpoint together with Aura.

blocks.cap: Dark and Darker. Image credit: IRONMACE

blocks.x: They ran things through a collaboration chat room, uploading example assets to a repository instead of writing documents. Since team members worked across different time zones, Park would log on in his own time zone, use Aura to catch up on what was newly added, and immediately start building content. Leaving a desired feature in the group chat usually meant the new feature was there by the next day.

For a few complex tutorial triggers that didn't get finished in time, Park had Aura write the code directly. The section of the tutorial where players learn to pick up bandages from a skeleton corpse was made that way.

blocks.cap: Dark and Darker. Image credit: IRONMACE

blocks.x: Verification and testing were still done by people inside the game editor. The UI widgets and logic connections Aura produced were usable, but artists handled the final polish.

“I believe in it now,” is Park's conclusion. An engineer who didn't know the codebase well built a substantial part of the basic system, and work expected to take 5-6 weeks was finished in half that time thanks to Aura.

blocks.cap: Ludo AI's Keyframe Animation. Image credit: PocketGamer.biz

blocks.x: Ludo AI has released Keyframe Animation, a tool that lets developers directly control AI-generated sprite animation, while also expanding its existing animation features covering both 2D and 3D assets.
It works in the Ludo app, the API, and the MCP server. Developers set up to three key poses, and Ludo fills in the frames in between.
One-click 3D rigging has also been added. It attaches an engine-ready skeleton to a model with no external software or manual work.

Developers set the start, middle, and end poses. They can use their own images or Ludo's built-in pose generation feature. Once the keyframes are set, a text prompt is optional, since the poses drive the animation instead.
Ludo AI said it generates up to 64 frames and lets users adjust length, size, and resolution. It supports character sprites, visual effects, and UI assets, and loops seamlessly by default.

Once a model is rigged, it can move using Ludo's library of ready-made motions. Users can also write out the motion they want in text to add custom motion. Custom animations come out in four variations, which can be previewed on the model before being exported as a single animation file.

Jorge Carvalho Gomes, co-founder and CTO of Ludo.ai, said: “Anyone can make sprite animation with AI now. That part is basically solved. The hard part is getting the exact animation you had in your head.”
“With Keyframe Animation, you don't describe a motion and hope it comes out right. You set the exact poses the animation will pass through, and Ludo fills in the rest.”

blocks.cap: Ryza in RyzaChat: AI. Image credit: Koei Tecmo

blocks.x: Koei Tecmo and Gust's Atelier series has exploded in popularity worldwide in recent years. Atelier Ryza's success and its heroine's design played a part; the team itself has admitted it made the character deliberately sensual to draw in more players. The developers moved on to other stories through several new titles without Ryza, but her popularity and look eventually made her the subject of Koei Tecmo's latest generative AI experiment: a plan to channel fans' parasocial feelings into a free-to-start AI chatbot RPG.

With more than half of Japanese game companies already experimenting with AI, it's not surprising that Koei Tecmo teamed up with Japanese AI startup Spiral AI to put out a project like this. The new mobile spinoff bundles that experiment into an AI RPG led by Ryza, the series' most beloved character: Ryza heading out on one more adventure, or simply Ryza as a conversation partner.

blocks.cap: RyzaChat: AI. Image credit: Koei Tecmo

blocks.x: RyzaChat: AI, released today in Japan for iOS and Android, returns to Kukkien Island, the setting of the original Atelier Ryza. Through an open-ended chatbot, players role-play what the developers describe as nearly endless, personalized generated quests with Ryza and other characters from the series. Besides the RPG mode, there is a “free chat” mode for getting to know Ryza through open-ended conversation. For those who want this character's synthetic voice whispering in their ear, there's even an ASMR mode.

The team calls this project an ethical AI adventure. Conversation logs from the game are not used to train future AI models, and Ryza's voice was trained solely on recordings from the original Japanese voice actor. No generative AI art or models were put into the game; the original artists returned to draw new art.

Even so, it runs on a subscription model with subscriber-only outfits like bikinis, and once the free tokens run out, continuing the conversation requires a separate payment. It's designed for a very narrow slice of the series' fans, and there is plenty of room for exploitation of people who become attached to companion Ryza.
A global release is also planned. The Japanese version of the app already supports several languages, including English, but an overseas release date has not yet been set.

blocks.cap: Crazy Taxi: World Tour. Image credit: Sega

blocks.x: Crazy Taxi: World Tour's multiplayer mode was revealed for the first time on Tuesday at Gamescom ONL. If AI use during development made it hard to fully welcome the revival of Sega's series, there's some good news: Sega has again clarified exactly where it used AI in developing Crazy Taxi, and while it's not perfect, it's a lot better than what was first known.

When that iconic “Yeah yeah yeah yeah yeah” played in the World Tour reveal trailer at the Xbox Games Showcase, I hit the ceiling right along with everyone else. Crazy Taxi was back, the soundtrack was intact, and the brief footage looked good.

The problem came right after. Once a game is revealed, the first thing people do these days is open its Steam page to check for AI disclosures. The World Tour page did in fact carry an AI use notice, and people who had been excited just minutes earlier turned against it.

blocks.cap: Crazy Taxi: World Tour. Image credit: Sega

blocks.x: The notice was even vague, confirming only that AI had not replaced the game's performers. Sega took note of the backlash and, as Automaton spotted, revised the AI disclosure on the World Tour page to spell out exactly how it used generative AI in development.

The bad news is that AI was used, and there's no getting around that. The good news is that it was used only “as part of the ideation process for background objects.” There's even better news: Sega has promised to remove all of the AI-generated content used to aid ideation, and whatever remains of it in those background objects, before the final version launches.

It's not perfect, but it's a big improvement over the earlier vague “AI was used.” It isn't clear exactly when Sega revised the wording; it may have been updated around a month ago. People only noticed on Tuesday, when they revisited the page after the new trailer dropped.

That puts World Tour alongside other games in recent years that used AI for ideation or placeholder material and got out without serious damage. Crimson Desert ran into trouble when Pearl Abyss left problematic AI art in the final game, and Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 lost an award it had won over similar AI use during development.

blocks.cap: Geoff Keighley on stage at Gamescom Opening Night Live. Image credit: TheGamer

blocks.x: This year's Gamescom Opening Night Live was a two-hour highlight reel of disappointment. Aside from the occasional item like Warlock: Dungeons & Dragons or Metro 2039, the biggest reveals were a remaster of a 10-year-old game and a remake of a 29-year-old one.
The showcase carried another kind of unease, too: a thin film of AI stretched over the whole thing.

It wasn't an illusion. Thirteen of the 55 games revealed — 23.64% — used AI somewhere in development or marketing. TheGamer combed through developer interviews, official blogs, and Steam disclosures for every reveal, and cross-checked the findings against a similar list posted by Reddit user FrostyMagazine9918.

1666 Amsterdam used AI placeholder assets in the game and in marketing, and Panache Digital said it would strip them out before launch. Aion 2 disclosed on Steam that AI generated some Arcana card designs and a number of icons. Ananta used AI for NPC interactions, and Aniimo used it in “multiple ways,” including testing. Crazy Taxi: World Tour used it “for reference” during development, and Like or Die used it “to assist with the creation of some assets.” Crimson Desert: Enhanced Edition had some AI used for placeholders carry over into the launch build.

Once Human uses AI-generated assets in its marketing. Petit Planet includes an AI chatbot, and HoYoverse has invested $14.6 billion in AI. PUBG Ded.Net wrote on Steam that it “uses AI tools to help develop some in-game content.” The Blood of the Dawnwalker's generative AI voice work is a placeholder, and Rebel Wolves said it will be replaced with actor voices before launch. Train Sim World 7 used ElevenLabs' text-to-speech for its announcements, and Zoopunk lets players use AI in customization.

blocks.cap: Image credit: Sega

blocks.x: 23.64% is a generous figure — it only counts games that admitted to using AI.

Capcom said it would use AI “aggressively” in development. Saber Interactive CEO Matthew Karch is an AI advocate, and the recently revealed Rideshare 'Stimulator' used AI-generated voice work for everything from missions to localized dialogue and music. Given the studios' interest, Monster Hunter Outlanders and Turok Origins likely used AI at some point in development too.

In many cases, AI was used only for placeholder assets — which is just as controversial among players. Placeholders aren't created in a vacuum; they're meant to give direction to the people building the final product. That's also why Larian Studios drew heavy scrutiny last year after admitting it used AI in the early stages of Divinity.

A recent BCG study found that 20% of new titles in Q3 2025 disclosed AI use, but the actual share of studios using AI in development is estimated at roughly half. Recalling that Geoff Keighley opened the showcase by mentioning soaring computing prices, it's rather ironic that the stage ended up filled with games that used AI.

blocks.cap: Grand Theft Auto VI. Image credit: GameSpot

blocks.x: Grand Theft Auto VI is the most anticipated game of the year, maybe of all time. Netflix aired a 27-minute extended trailer, and a wave of coverage followed. Several outlets visited Rockstar North in Scotland, and according to one of them, GTA VI will have no microtransactions at launch and was developed without generative AI.

On the Kinda Funny Gamecast, Andy Cortez and Greg Miller asked Rockstar North co-studio head Rob Nelson two questions: whether there's room for microtransactions in GTA, and whether generative AI was used in development. Both said the answer was simply “no.”
“Can you buy things in the game with real money? No monetization.” That's Cortez. Miller followed up: “We asked point blank. 'Is there AI in the game?' No AI.”

The lack of generative AI also appears in The New York Times' Grand Theft Auto VI feature, published the same day. Citing Rockstar, the article said GTA VI's animations number well over 600,000. Grand Theft Auto V had 55,000, and Red Dead Redemption 2 had 300,000. The article also confirmed that Rockstar emphasized the new game's “handcrafted” work.

blocks.cap: Image credit: Meta

blocks.x: Meta has released Meta XR Operator, an experimental tool that lets AI coding agents build, test, and debug VR apps on their own, and then check the screen to confirm the result.

Developers have already sped up reading and writing code with AI agents, and running tests and fixing bugs was no different. What was missing was a step that confirmed whether any of it actually worked.
XR Operator is an OpenXR API layer. It ships as an experimental-stage component in Meta XR SDK v205.

Any agent that supports the Model Context Protocol (MCP) can see, move through, and interact with a VR app running in the Meta XR Simulator. According to Meta, the agent can build and run a Unity scene directly, take screenshots to spot problems, fix them, and then confirm the fix is correct.
Natural-language testing is included too. A developer writes out a test scenario in words, the agent runs it as written, and returns pass/fail evidence with screenshots attached.

Early testing involved teams building with the Meta XR SDK, including Beat Games, the studio behind Beat Saber. One of the earliest experiments was building a tic-tac-toe app in VR: the agent wrote the game logic, aimed a virtual controller at a square, pressed the A button to place a mark, and played the board out until the game was won or lost.

It isn't a complete verification tool. It can't hear sound, and it can't properly judge animation or motion. It also can't use finger-level tracking and will miss subtle visual flaws. It's too slow to keep up with real-time interaction, so it struggles with moving controls too. Meta said it works best in “static, deterministic scenarios.”

Support is still narrow, too. It only runs on the Meta XR Core SDK for Unity. For other OpenXR engines like Godot or Unreal Engine, developers have to download a standalone package and wire it in themselves.

Road to VR sees Meta as positioning itself to “build a better shovel” rather than mine the gold itself — a different choice from the approach it took from the Rift era in 2016 through the end of this spring with Quest, buying up VR studios and pouring millions of dollars into exclusive content. More of the story is expected at Meta Connect 2026, which opens September 22.

Early results from AI game development are already showing up. Indie modders are using AI to bring flat PC games into VR, and the list keeps growing by the day. With a lower barrier to entry, mods are coming out better and faster.

blocks.cap: From left: Teppei Tachibana, Benedikte Mikkelsen, Martin McBride, Christoffer Holmgård. Image credit: Modl.ai/Side

blocks.x: Game services company Side has signed a memorandum of understanding with Danish AI firm Modl.ai. The binding agreement runs six months, during which the two companies will build an AI-based quality assurance system together. Side has long operated in the services market under the name PTW, while Modl.ai is a newer company, founded in 2018 and having raised $1.7 million in seed funding two years later.

Martin McBride, Side's chief commercial officer, said that “what's currently considered the crown jewel, the holy grail, in the games industry is better augmenting QA services with AI technology.” “Nobody has really cracked it. We think we have.”

Earlier AI QA technology only worked if developers handed over the entire build. Modl.ai's previous approach was also “integration-based,” attaching plugins and SDKs, which required source code. Friction was high, and as founder Christoffer Holmgard put it, “it got harder over time.”

The new system doesn't look inside. “We take the product as-is, as if we were handing it to a QA tester, and put it on a similar or identical device. Then our solution looks at the screen and plays the game, simulating key flows, and turns everything that happens into a dataset. A second AI system goes through that, finds bugs, escalates them to a human level, and asks whether they need action,” Holmgard explained.

The first step is building what Modl.ai calls “game knowledge.” Developers upload project assets and talk with the AI. “It's all done in natural language. Sometimes images get attached, sometimes game design documents get uploaded.” Next comes deciding what to test, a stage that still needs human expertise to refine the prompts so the agent behaves correctly.

After that, the system turns the data from a single run into a bug report. “We get all the text, along with what we call evidence — short clips and log data. That goes to a human QA expert. That person reviews it and decides how it gets handled in the rest of production.” The sense of what counts as a bug versus a feature in a given game also seeps into the system as tester feedback accumulates.

Side envisions a future where QA staff move into AI engineering roles. McBride said “the nice thing about programs like this is that it moves our people up the value chain.” Instead of climbing from tester to senior tester, someone becomes an AI engineer, gets paid more for it, and that also opens room to bring jobs back to countries they'd left because of labor costs.

Benedikte Mikkelsen, Modl.ai's chief product officer, pointed to cutting out repetition. “You don't need a person to repeat the same flow over and over. That person can do far more valuable work.” McBride was also clear that AI doesn't replace QA staff. Side sees AI as a “sliding scale.” “Humans will always be in the loop. That's our ethos.”

Still, the games this technology can currently handle are limited. Side's chief operating officer Oliver Deslandes was candid: “Puzzle games, card games, things that aren't too fast. Things with repeatable mechanics. Something very fast like a fighting game is more of a later conversation.” It's aimed at small experiences rather than 3D open worlds.

blocks.cap: Tencent Games Central Tech. Image credit: Tencent Games

blocks.x: Tencent Games Central Tech made its first appearance as a unified brand at Gamescom. It brought out its own bundle of technologies spanning content creation, gameplay experience, and long-term live operations. On the Gamescom 2026 showcase stage were Motus, GIGA, MagicDawn, Anti-Cheat Expert, GVoice, and WeTest.

At the center is Motus, an AI pipeline that handles 3D character animation start to finish, built on top of Tencent's own generative animation foundation model. It links together rigging, skinning, motion generation, motion correction, and real-time character interaction, processes that used to run separately.

blocks.cap: Motus, the 3D character animation pipeline. Image credit: Tencent Games

blocks.x: Motion can be generated from text prompts, video, or keyframes. Multi-character interaction covers combat, cooperation, and even social gestures. It analyzes character topology to produce a production-ready skeleton within seconds and attaches skinning weights to areas like muscles and clothing.

It isn't just a generation tool. Its correction features find and fix problems like jitter, mesh penetration, joint anomalies, and foot sliding on their own. At the end of the pipeline, audio or text drives facial expressions, gestures, and reactions in real time. Tencent has intelligent NPCs, digital humans, and even virtual hosts in mind.

Zijiao Zeng, Motus's technical lead and principal researcher, explained the pipeline on August 24 at Gamescom Dev's “Breathing Life into Geometry 2.0” session, where a demo turning text prompts into 3D animation was also shown live. According to Tencent, Motus technology has already been used in Game for Peace, PUBG MOBILE, Delta Force, Honor of Kings, Roco Kingdom, League of Legends, and Teamfight Tactics.

blocks.cap: The Gamescom 2026 floor. Image credit: Tencent Games

blocks.x: The Central Tech lineup reaches beyond animation. GIGA uses games and virtual worlds as a training ground for general-purpose AI agents, focusing on vision-based decision-making, aligning language with behavior, and real-time competitive behavior. MagicDawn layers AI and cloud computing onto rendering technology to handle performance, visual quality, and audio. Tencent cited Roco Kingdom as an example, saying global illumination and cross-platform support let the browser game move into a 64-square-kilometer open world.

blocks.cap: MagicDawn, which layers AI and cloud onto rendering. Image credit: Tencent Games

blocks.x: Anti-Cheat Expert handles cheat blocking, client protection, in-game economic risk, and threat intelligence. GVoice is low-latency voice communication with AI noise removal, its own codec, and real-time translation. WeTest Acorn AI Studio has autonomous agents play games directly, finding problems across genres and platforms.

The message Tencent put forward at Gamescom 2026 is that these technologies are moving past demo showcases to become reusable parts of real development pipelines. Research on world models and real-time interactive video continues as well. Tencent hasn't yet said which games will use the technology going forward.

Dr. Yanpei Cao, co-founder and chief scientist of Tripo, talked about Smart Mesh, how to produce usable topology in seconds, Gaussian splats, and the shift from generating a single asset to a complete interactive world.

Generating a 3D model from a single image has gotten much easier in the past few years. The problem is that the result isn't immediately usable. Messy topology, materials that are hard to touch up, and uneven geometry mean a lot of cleanup has to happen before it can go into a pipeline.

Dr. Cao studied geometry processing and reconstruction at Tsinghua University and co-founded Owlii, which was later acquired by Kuaishou. He became convinced then that slow, fragmented 3D production was a bottleneck, and when generative AI appeared, he decided to build a platform that would lower the barrier to entry.

Tripo Smart Mesh, released this year, draws on the SIGGRAPH research Nexus. From a single image, it produces game-ready assets with clean edge flow instead of polygon soup. Results come back end-to-end in under 5 seconds, so developers can throw out 20 or 50 prompts and pick a direction a few seconds later. The output goes straight into Blender, Maya, or Unity.

Input can be a single line of text, several reference images, or an entire character sheet. There's also a way to refine geometry and textures directly with a Magic Brush. TripoSplat, released under an MIT license, was supported by Comfy from day one.

Generating a finished character takes under a minute with the high-resolution H series, and under 10 seconds with Smart Mesh. Polygon counts come out around 20,000, and the edge flow is usable as is. Billing is token-based.

Dr. Cao named three things as the next homework: moving from a single asset to environments and interaction, attaching the code and logic that build environments, and a world model that predicts the next few minutes. Once those three come together, artists will spend their time setting direction instead of making assets and writing scripts.

blocks.cap: Key art for the Myth and Magic update. A dwarf mage casts a spell beneath the form of Armok. Image credit: Kitfox Games

blocks.x: Dwarf Fortress has already implemented cat alcoholism, procedurally generated bardic traditions, and thermonuclear dragon breath that goes off like a time bomb. But brothers and developers Tarn Adams and Zach Adams haven't let go of an even bigger goal: magic. Procedural magic tied to a cosmology and mythology that gets rewritten every time a player hits 'generate new world,' and that only works within that particular world.

It's a reckless undertaking even for a game that already set the bar for simulation complexity. It took 10 years and required overhauling the entire scripting system. Putnam, the first programmer Bay 12 Games hired from outside the Adams brothers, carried that work. It's honestly hard to believe, but the first piece arrives this year.

In a short announcement video, Tarn Adams confirmed the first Myth and Magic update arrives this year. He said the goal is a procedural magic system that reaches past combining spell effects and digs straight into a universe's fundamental cosmological makeup, creating magical situations that couldn't come about any other way.

The idea dates back to 2017. By tying magic to each world's creation myth and cosmology, Dwarf Fortress stops being a game that stamps out world variations and becomes a generator that creates entire fantasy settings. The result is universes where magic is as fundamental as the laws of physics.
Adams said: “It allows your fortresses to pursue magical research that really feels like discovery.” That means your fortress can carry out magical research that genuinely feels like discovery.

blocks.cap: A six-armed fly-man clears a corridor full of goblins with magic. Image credit: Kitfox Games

blocks.x: The video is only a minute long, but it offers glimpses of characters using magic. A goblin shaman teleports a cat, a dwarf mage repeatedly slams a goblin into a wall, and a six-armed fly-man holding four wands tears through a corridor full of enemy swordsmen with a barrage of magic bolts. A dwarf cursed with undeath by a necromancer immediately starts biting the comrade next to it.

Over a scene of a magic projectile quickly demolishing a dwarven outpost, Adams added that there will be magic effects that blow things up, but also everything that makes fantasy feel like fantasy: magical materials, enchantments, rituals, and ancient ruins. And each one is tied to how that particular universe works at its core.
There's no release date yet for the first Myth and Magic update. Dwarf Fortress is currently available on Steam and the Bay 12 Games site.

blocks.cap: Games unfairly suspected of using genAI. Image credit: Rock Paper Shotgun

blocks.x: Witch hunts over whether art used in a game is the output of generative AI have become routine. Over several weeks, Rock Paper Shotgun spoke with developers and artists who were unfairly singled out and asked why that particular image drew suspicion. AI images have no fixed style or quality; the result is shaped entirely by what was fed into the model, so any detection trick that worked once quickly goes stale.

Hannah Flynn, communications director at Failbetter, maker of Fallen London, said that whenever a video goes viral or there's a major announcement, the question of whether they use genAI always follows. The studio has even posted a statement on its homepage saying it won't use AI. Her guess is that a painterly art style, or odd bodily details like too many eyes or fingers, actually invite more suspicion.

blocks.cap: A monster with a candle on its head. A scene from the horror game Tenebris Somnia. Image credit: New Blood Interactive

blocks.x: David Oshry, CEO of New Blood Interactive, faced the same suspicion over Tenebris Somnia, a horror game that mixes pixel art with live-action footage. He ended up having to release a separate behind-the-scenes video showing how the props were made. He said the criticism, especially on Instagram, is almost constant now; a year ago this kind of reaction was rare. The uproar did boost the wishlist by 15,000 adds in a single week.

Abandoned Sheep, maker of Schrodinger's Cat Burglar, ended up replacing the art entirely. The key art in question was hand-drawn by local artist Tom Williams in mid-2022, before genAI could produce that level of quality. Studio director Martin Binfield said it seems to have been flagged for looking too polished. The comments leaned less toward “is this AI?” and more toward a flat assertion that they wouldn't buy it until the AI was removed.

blocks.cap: The old key art for Schrodinger's Cat Burglar, repeatedly singled out as AI-generated. Image credit: Abandoned Sheep

blocks.x: Illustrator Janna Sophia Koppenwallner is writing her master's thesis on how accurately people can spot AI. The data is still preliminary and not yet peer-reviewed, but average detection accuracy came out to 74%, and people who completed a short training module actually did slightly worse. She added that the art most often mistaken for AI tended to be clean, highly polished, popular styles. The more data available, the better a model can reproduce a style, so niche styles still can't be convincingly imitated.

The texture of the mistakes differs too. AI blends things together, like hair flowing into a necklace, because it's stitching things together by probability without knowing what it's actually drawing. A human beginner's mistakes don't look like that.

blocks.cap: A 10-panel image showing path tracing and denoising applied step by step. Image credit: Abdou Bouam

blocks.x: Things get more tangled when older machine-learning tools enter the picture. Freelance artist Abdou Bouam was asked by a client whether a blurry smudge was AI; it was actually a denoising artifact. Path-traced renders start out full of noise and only become physically accurate once enough samples accumulate. Denoisers like Nvidia Optix, which came out in 2018, do use machine learning, but they're a different thing from today's generative AI: they were trained on images rendered with deliberately added noise rather than scraped data, and they run locally rather than in a data center.

Koppenwallner said pure visual detection is only getting harder. These days the real clues lie more in context than in the image itself. Knowing that, and using it to protect yourself, is different from trusting a gut feeling and publicly calling someone out.

blocks.cap: An excerpt from Google Cloud's blog post 'Level up: How AI is unlocking a new golden age of games.' Image credit: Aftermath

blocks.x: The Aftermath writer said they wasted a few minutes of their life reading Google Cloud's company blog post 'Level up: How AI is unlocking a new golden age of games.' The author is Jack Buser, Google's global director of games.

The shape of it is predictable: a sales pitch written by someone from the company, followed by sentences that read like LinkedIn bait. “We need a structural shift to revive the ecosystem where creative risks are sustainable again. Fortunately, AI has matured enough to help drive that renaissance.” In other words, reviving the ecosystem so creative risk-taking becomes sustainable again requires a structural shift, and fortunately AI has matured enough to help drive that renaissance.

What actually caught the writer's eye was the end of the post. Buser cites three cases he calls 'interesting' uses of AI in game development: Chatty Slimey, a real-time multimodal companion Square Enix is adding to Dragon Quest X Online; The Ritual, a custom generation system from 10Six Games' time-traveling horde-survival roguelite YOU vs. Zombies, which launched this summer; and Teammates, Ubisoft's prototype that replaces command menus with voice direction.

The writer's response is short and harsh: after three to four years poured into this collective madness, is this trio of minor, annoying, unpopular party tricks really all you have to back up a sales pitch? They ask whether this is really what Google means by a golden age.

The only thing Chatty Slimey seems to be building with the Dragon Quest fandom is how much people dislike it. YOU vs. Zombies, which the writer had never heard of before and looked up, looks poor. Teammates has already shown up once before, in an Aftermath piece from November 2025.

Developers and studios that bet everything on AI pipelines have spent years at it. And still there's no output that makes an ordinary person care about this technology.
